definition: A legally enforceable promise or set of promises between two or more competent parties to do or not do something lawful.
Competent parties, offer and acceptance (mutual assent), consideration, and a legal purpose. Real estate sale contracts must also be in writing and signed.
Something of legal value exchanged by the parties, such as money, a promise, or an act.
An agreement with no legal effect from the start, such as one with an illegal purpose.
A contract that is valid until the party with the right to cancel chooses to do so, such as one signed by a minor or under duress.
A contract that appears valid but cannot be enforced in court, such as an oral agreement to sell land.
The law requiring certain contracts, including contracts to sell real estate, to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
A contract in which both parties exchange promises, such as a purchase agreement.
A contract in which only one party makes a promise and the other may act to accept, such as an option.
A contract that has not yet been fully performed, such as a purchase agreement before closing.
A contract that both parties have fully performed.
A contract whose terms are stated in words, either written or spoken.
A contract created by the parties' conduct rather than by stated words.
Transferring your rights under a contract to someone else. The original party usually stays liable unless released.
Replacing an old contract or party with a new one, which releases the original party from liability.
Canceling a contract and returning the parties to where they were before it was made.
A court order requiring a party to do what the contract says, often used in real estate because every parcel is unique.
Money a court awards to cover the actual loss caused by a breach.
An amount agreed to in advance as the damages for a breach, often the buyer's earnest money.
Failure to perform a contract obligation without a legal excuse.
A clause requiring deadlines in the contract to be met exactly. Missing one is a breach.
The time limit set by law for filing a lawsuit.
An employment contract between a property owner and a broker to market the property.
A listing in which the broker earns a commission no matter who sells the property, including the owner.
A listing with one broker, but the owner owes no commission if the owner finds the buyer without help.
A nonexclusive listing the owner may give to several brokers. Only the broker who is the procuring cause is paid.
A listing in which the broker keeps everything above the seller's stated net. Illegal or discouraged in many states because of the conflict of interest.
The broker whose efforts started an unbroken chain of events that resulted in the sale.
A listing clause that entitles the broker to a commission if the property sells after expiration to a buyer the broker introduced during the listing.
A cooperative database where member brokers share listings.
A written contract creating an agency relationship between a buyer and a broker, stating the broker's duties and compensation.
A buyer agreement in which the buyer works with only one broker, who is paid if the buyer purchases during the term.
A buyer agreement that lets the buyer work with other brokers. The broker is paid only if they are the procuring cause.
A written agreement in which a broker represents a person looking to lease property.
A proposal by one party (offeror) to enter a contract on stated terms.
The offeree's unconditional agreement to every term of an offer, communicated to the offeror.
A response that changes any term of an offer. It rejects the original offer and becomes a new offer.
A deposit the buyer makes to show good faith. It is held in trust and usually applied to the purchase price at closing.
A condition that must be met before a contract becomes binding or must be performed, such as financing or inspection.
A buyer's interest in property after signing a purchase agreement but before receiving legal title.
The person who makes an offer.
The person to whom an offer is made.
A contract in which an owner (optionor) gives another (optionee) the right to buy or lease at set terms within a set time, for consideration.
The owner who grants an option and is bound to sell if the option is exercised.
The person who holds an option and may choose whether to exercise it.
A right to buy or lease a property by matching another offer before the owner accepts it.
A seller-financed sale where the buyer pays in installments and gets possession, but the seller keeps legal title until paid. Also called a contract for deed or installment contract.
In a land contract, the vendor is the seller who keeps legal title, and the vendee is the buyer who holds equitable title.
